en: Exposition of the "Chapter on Expedient Means," composed by the Tang Dynasty Tiantai monk Zhìràn. Regarding the "Exposition of the Chapter on Expedient Means":

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Zhèngfǎhuá jīng) titles this chapter "The Chapter on Skillful Means" (*Shànquán pǐn*). Furthermore, throughout the explanatory text, it consistently refers to it as "Skillful Means."

Regarding "expedient means" (upāya), one should know that Dharmarakṣa also explains expedient means through skillful means (kauśalya); "skill" (shan) is merely another name for "ingenuity" (qiao). The text is divided into two parts;

the first is a brief explanation, which itself contains two sub-sections. Within the first sub-section, the formal explanation itself consists of three parts: the first follows the etymological definition of the characters, while the latter two follow the meaning and significance.
Furthermore, the first two [interpretations] derive from ancient teachings, while the last one belongs to the present sutra.

Although there are three explanations, all take the three vehicles as their provisional means (*upāya*); they differ only in terms of being able to lead across or not being able to lead across, and whether they are identical with or distinct from [the ultimate]. One must briefly discuss the general purport of these three types before one can properly interpret the text.

However, among these three, the first is designated by the name of the "Three Teachings" based on the capacity to employ them; herein, the Dharma is that which is employed, and the employment is the capacity to employ. Although both the Dharma and the employment pertain to all four teachings, there is a distinction between the square and the round, and between divergence and convergence. Thus, the designation "expedient means" (upāya) is established based on the provisional; since the provisional is not identical to the real, it is distinguished from the past. To establish a substantial body outside of the provisional is not the intent of this present chapter. Within the text, citing the "round" refers specifically to the ultimate reality, as it is presented in contrast to the former.

Therefore, we know that in the past, the profound and subtle was not explained as being the "expedient means" (upāya); rather, it was precisely because it was kept secret and not taught that it was termed "expedient means.
Furthermore, the "perfect" (yuan) of the past was merely a "concurrent" perfection; thus, neither the universal nor the perfect accord with the intent of the present [teaching].

Next, the second interpretation holds that "expedient" (*upāya*) belongs to the capacity to penetrate the three teachings and may also be termed "skillful means. However, although this is not identical [to the ultimate], it serves as a remote designation for the Perfect; and since the Perfect which is designated also carries the connotation of its designator as "expedient," one should know that neither of these interpretations accords with the intent of the present chapter.

The previous explanation did not state that the three are "capable" because the provisional and the real meet at their respective extremes, and thus their methods differ; it was only in the third explanation that the three provisional [truths] were shown to be identical to the one real truth. It is by pointing to these provisional means as being precisely the real that they are designated as the "expedient means" (*upāya*) of this present sutra.
Next, regarding the exegesis of the text, the first section—concerning the application of the Dharma—is divided into five parts:

first, the Dharma itself; second, the presentation of a simile; third, the clarification of the intent behind employing skillful means (*upāya*); fourth, the citation of scriptural evidence; and fifth, the conclusion of the refutation from the words "This meaning" onwards.
The first section also has three parts;
first, the explanation of the definition.
Regarding the phrase "Fang means fa (dharma)," the *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"Law (fa) is technique (shu).
This corresponds to the current text. The *Erya* says:
"It is the 'ze' (standard).
This refers to the "ze" of the Legalist school.
It further states:
"It is correct. Now it is likewise so; because its Dharma is correct, one may then adapt to the capacities of beings, and though it has not yet been fully revealed, it cannot but be correct.
Next, from "The Dharma exists" onwards, the meaning is explained.
Although both involve the functioning of the Dharma, when the partial is compared to the perfect, the partial deviates while the perfect attains realization;
though realization is superior to deviation, realization itself is not deviation, for its functioning reveals that it is not merely marvelous.
Third, the explanation of the characteristics under "The Three Expedients" is further divided into two parts:

first, the explanation of the squareness and roundness of the Dharma, which distinguishes between the partial and the perfect by contrasting them with the compass and square, thereby demonstrating that [the former] is not wondrous.

Regarding "three sides and one circle," although all four teachings are equally termed "dharma-function" (dharmopāya), it is specifically the partial dharmas that are designated as "expedient means" (upāya).
Next, from "If wisdom... onwards, the differences and convergence of these functions are explained.
The reason both are designated as "Dharma" and "application" (*yòng*) is that each accords with a specific capacity.
It is not because they both meet the Perfect [Teaching] that they are both called "adapted" (*dòu*).

Furthermore, regarding "Dharma" and "application": although the name "Dharma" is universal, since its application is adapted to the timing and is not yet uniform, one must consider which Dharma is used to adapt to which capacity.

Therefore, because these four methods respond to capacities with varying degrees of correspondence, the provisional and the real stand in mutual relation, and both the right and the wrong are ultimately negated.

As previously explained, since the intent of the Dharma has not yet been fully integrated, its application to beings has not yet been thoroughly expressed, and the established rules remain distinct; thus, for now, it is merely called "skillful use."
"Attaining" (yì) refers to that which is reached; it is precisely the application [of the Dharma].
Since the attainments of wisdom differ, the applications of the Dharma are not equal.

Regarding the meaning of the subsequent analogy: it primarily illustrates the differences in the application of the Dharma. Within this, there are two layers of dharma-analogies. In the midst of these, the name "method of the Perfect" (yuánzhōng fāngfǎ) is set aside, and instead the designation "secret and wondrous" (bìmì) is borrowed. Thus, even within the Perfect that transcends the partial (biān), there is a skillful means within the essence of the body (tǐnèi fāngbiàn); therefore, it is called "secret and wondrous."
The name "secret and wondrous" (mi-miao) appears similar to that used for the third [teaching], yet their meanings differ. Why?

Because in the third [teaching], it is the act of revealing and manifesting that constitutes the "wondrous," whereas here, it is the unique and perfect nature itself that constitutes the "wondrous. Thus, within this text, while all four methods are present, the first three teachings are merely called "methods"; they are neither secret nor wondrous. Only the subsequent Perfect Teaching is both secret and wondrous; therefore, the name "secret and wondrous" applies specifically to the latter teaching and does not pertain to the act of revealing. Consequently, employing a partial method is like pointing a single finger toward only one direction.
If one employs the Perfect Teaching (yuanfa), it is like using all five fingers to point toward all directions.

Regarding the meaning of employing provisional means (quan): prior to that [attainment of the Perfect], what was not yet in accord with reality was termed "acting according to desire" by means of provisional teachings.

Fourth, regarding the citation of evidence: one should take the three provisional [teachings] as the means for leading forth [beings]. Because the text relies on parables, it speaks of "the triple world"; furthermore, that which is to be abandoned is not distinct from the triple world. Since the Tathāgata’s skillful means are fundamentally one, this meaning has not yet been proclaimed; therefore, it belongs to the teachings of the past.

Although these are expedient means external to the essence, they are not non-internal to the principle; yet sentient beings do not yet know this. Therefore, speaking according to the Buddha’s intention, it is called "praising expedient means," but because [the ultimate truth] has not yet been revealed, this is not the intended meaning of the present chapter.

Next, regarding the second point concerning the expressive (the *nirukta*): if one considers the relationship between principle (*tattva*) and teaching (*śāsana*), all four teachings, when discussed individually, are none other than the expressive. Now, however, when the three are compared with the one, the three serve as the expression for the reality of the one; therefore, the three are termed "the expressive. Consequently, within the aforementioned three teachings, both the teaching (*dharma*), the practice (*pratipatti*), and the principle (*tattva*) are all considered the expressive.
This section consists of seven parts.
First, the three teachings are established uprightly as the gates; this is an explanation based on their meaning rather than a lexical definition.

Next, from the phrase "The Name of the Gates" onward, the meaning of "gate" (*mukha*) is explained: just as a gate in the world exists fundamentally for the purpose of providing passage, these three [teachings] are called gates because they all lead into reality.

Third, the section on "Expedient Means" (*upāya*) below clarifies the intent of the gate: sentient beings do not realize that [the means] are originally what is to be penetrated; rather, based on their attachments, they achieve what is merely a deceptive lure (*nongyin*). However, those who are unskillful and crooked take the lure itself to be the deception.
4. From "True Reality" (*tattva*) downward, the function of the gate is clarified; although it is not identical with that which is attained, entry is achieved by means of this.

5. From "From the Capable" (*śakta*) downward, the derivation of the name is clarified; since the provisional and the real are still separated due to differences in the capacities of sentient beings, the previous two explanations—pertaining to the manifest aspect and the stages prior to the distinct grounds—are not the intended meaning of this chapter.

The intent of citing these six proofs is to clarify that while those former gates were merely described as "able to lead through," they must now be opened; therefore, it is said that "the gate of expedient means is opened. This does not mean that the opening of the gate was already explained therein.
7. Regarding the phrase "This meaning" below, it concludes the refutation.

As for the third interpretation, this is the intended meaning of the present chapter; however, the previous two interpretations were merely termed "partial gates" (piānmén) in the past and were kept secret without being taught.
Now, by opening those partial gates, they become the locus of the Perfect (yuán); therefore, it is called "secret and wondrous" (bìmì).
Because it is revealed and made manifest, it is called "truly secret.
Furthermore, there are six [aspects].
First, regarding "standing upright": that which was secret in the past has now been opened, and thus that very secret becomes wondrous in the present.

Next, regarding the explanation of the function [of the teaching] starting from "subtly penetrating" (*miaoda*): "penetrating" (*da*) refers to the expedient means of opening up the subtlety; because one opens the secret method and there is no dharma outside of this subtlety, it is said to be "identical" (*jishi*).

Third, regarding the section "Pointing Within" (*diǎn nèi*), which uses the teaching for people to demonstrate the characteristics: within the bodies of sentient beings there exists the causal conditions of past seeds, termed the "pearl in the garment. Since their own retrogression, they have been like those intoxicated guests; even the name "partial gate" does not exist for them, let alone the "perfect" [gate].

If this were not revealed, the three provisional means would remain unmanifest, like a pearl covered by a garment; now that the present sutra reveals them, they become one with the wisdom of fruition. One should understand that the same applies to the person who acts [as the Buddha].
4. From "In this manner" onwards is the conclusion of the title; since the methods and gates are secret and subtle, it says "in this manner.
5. From "As the sūtra says" onwards is the citation of evidence.
Sixth, from "Therefore, by means of" onwards, the title is concluded and its identity is revealed.
Next, within the section on analytical examination, there are three parts:

first, regarding the three types of speech concerning self and others, it relies upon the previous first interpretation to distinguish between the three; thus, that which is initially opened up is the third [category].
Next, regarding the subject and object, the second explanation is cited to distinguish it from the three [previous] texts; thus, the second which is opened up is also the third.
Thirdly, by means of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), all three explanations are collectively distinguished.

Regarding the first explanation, there are three texts. To distinguish the first text: the three teachings are consistently termed "other" and "provisional," because the provisional obstructs the real.
Regarding the second text: it contrasts the "other" of the three teachings with the "self" of the Perfect Teaching.

To explain the third passage: within the substance of the three together, there is nothing that is not real; they are merely designated as "self" and "self," with no "other" existing externally—the same applies to the term "three.

Next, regarding the subject and object, there are likewise three passages, all employing the two characters "subject" (neng) and "object" (suo) to distinguish between what is correct and incorrect regarding the subject and object.

To explain the first passage: for the time being, let us consider the Three Teachings; since even their functional application (*dharmopayoga*) is not yet capable of true penetration, how much less so the object of that penetration?
Therefore, the Three Teachings are neither the subject nor the object [of ultimate penetration], and thus all three provisional means (*upāya*) are entirely coarse.

To explain the next point: the "gates" refer to the three teachings, which possess the capacity to lead [to enlightenment]; however, because it is not stated that the three teachings are themselves the Perfect Teaching, they are not what is ultimately penetrated. Since they are not identical [to the ultimate], they remain coarse.

To explain the third passage: it also opens up the preceding two [categories]. That which is neither agent nor object, as well as that which is capable of penetration, together constitute the object; within this object, skillfulness is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*). Therefore, wondrous expedient means differs from both "method" and the "gate of penetration."

The section beginning with "Therefore we know" concludes the refutation. First, it summarizes whether the names and essences are identical or different; although both are termed "expedient means," even if there are these three differences, how could one understand their meanings merely by hearing the names?
Therefore, all three interpretations contain words of expedient means (*upāya*), yet two of them do not belong to the present chapter; hence it is said that "the meanings differ.
The passage beginning with "The people of the world" generally rebukes worldly people; how could the Great Master harbor partiality or favoritism based on biased attachments?
What of the principle?
What of the letter? What of the practice?
As for how this accords with realization:

Master Sengsheng was naturally gifted and uniquely eminent, yet he still remarked that [the Buddha] had "bestowed titles from of old. If these were titles bestowed from of old, for what reason did he offer such praise?
If one praises the past, does this not constitute a disparagement of the present?

If one praises the present by means of the past, one loses the significance of the past; thus, the provisional power within the essence would be entirely lacking, and the function outside the essence would be deficient, resulting in the loss of both the internal and the external. How, then, could one praise the Buddha’s provisional wisdom?

If the manifestation by the five Buddhas were merely redundant with the initial bestowal, and the skillful means of the three assemblies were still in vain, then to claim that although the chapter is titled as from the past, its substance exists in the present, would be like hanging a signboard for a district while confusing the practitioner.

Furthermore, in the first explanation, since the three [aspects] such as "conforming to others" were already used to connect with the latter two explanations, and the subsequent explanation further uses "gate" (*mukha*) to connect the beginning and the end, it follows by logic that "wondrous" (*miau*) should also connect with the former two; that it is absent from the text is merely an abbreviation, indicated simply by the note "and so forth" (*yún yún*). One should say: in the first explanation, the skillful means (*upāya*) are secret but not wondrous; in the second explanation, the skillful means are secret and capable of entering the wondrous; in the final explanation, the skillful means being secret is itself the wondrous. This was spoken from the perspective of the Buddha’s internal realization; now, because they have become manifest (*prakaṭa*), they are omitted and not discussed.

Regarding the first question within the fourfold analysis: since the *Zheng* edition reads "skillful means" (*upāya*), one should know that "means" (*quan*) is a synonym for "expedient means" (*fangbian*). Because the intention is to examine the similarities and differences between these synonyms, the question is first raised.

The answer consists of four parts: first, the presentation and enumeration; second, the explanation; third, the judgment from the section beginning with "three phrases"; and fourth, the citation of evidence from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

In the explanation, the pair of "mutual subversion" (*xiāngpò*) is divided into two phrases, while "mutual cultivation" (*xiāngxiū*) and "mutual identity" (*xiāngjí*) each constitute one phrase; thus, there are four phrases in total.

Other texts may treat these as three phrases or six phrases, depending on how the intent is established according to their respective doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), yet the structural arrangement of the phrases remains constant.

Having now established three pairs, they are then expanded into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); this is done so that the four propositions may be used to correspond with the three explanations, with the first three propositions being assigned to the first two explanations.
If there were only three phrases, what would be wrong with assigning the first two phrases to the first two categories?
It is simply because their textual characteristics differ within the section on mutual refutation (*xiangpo*).

Furthermore, according to the principle of mutual refutation, the section on mutual cultivation (*xiangxiu*) could likewise be divided into two phrases; thus, assigning all four phrases to the preceding [two] categories would not constitute a major error. Names and phrases are applied according to the occasion and cannot be standardized in every instance.

Regarding the term "mutually subverting": provisional and expedient teachings have both names—partial and perfect—throughout both the past and the present. In the past, these two names, partial and perfect, were mutually subverting; in the present, however, the names and the essence of the partial and perfect are identical. This is called "mutually subverting" in contrast to the initial explanation.
In the present age, the three teachings are equally wondrous; they are called "provisional" (*upāya*) and also called "expedient means" (*upāyakauśalya*).

In the past, all three were equally coarse; they were also called "provisional" and "expedient means. Therefore, by using the two [teachings] of the past to mutually refute each other, two phrases are established. Thus, the three teachings of the two *sūtras* (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Nirvāṇa*) are contrasted with the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). Consequently, within the past teachings, these three become both "secret and wondrous" and "of the same essence" (*samātman*) for those of the Perfect Teaching; hence it is said: "All four kinds are secret and wondrous, as well as of the same essence."
Therefore, the previous statements of mutual refutation were based merely on names and not on the actual substance; now, by following the names, we explain that their substance is eternally fixed.

As for the statement regarding "mutual cultivation," these two names were also established alternately in the past within the [first] two teachings; however, it is the two names of the Perfect Teaching that mutually cultivate one another. For this reason, it differs from the preceding sentences of mutual refutation.

Although those of the Perfect Teaching (the *en-jin*) in the past also perceived all four [teachings] as equally secret and wondrous, they could not explicitly state the words that they are mutually identical within that teaching; therefore, they merely relied on the previous comparative analysis. Thus, regarding the mutual cultivation (*xiangxiu*), one also distinguishes the One Perfect Teaching by contrasting it with the three other teachings.

Why is this? If one abandons the three [vehicles] and cultivates the perfect [vehicle], it is the same as the first phrase; if one realizes that the three are themselves the perfect, it is the same as the latter phrase. By neither abandoning nor identifying with them, one enters from the provisional into the real, and thus attains the name "cultivation."

If, prior to that, regarding the two flavors and three teachings, bodhisattvas of sharp faculties attain them through the manifest teaching, while the two vehicles of the two teachings attain them only through the secret teaching; because they enter by means of these, they are called "gates."

Regarding the statement that "the characteristics are identical," this refers precisely to the opening [of the gates]. Therefore, the mutual sublation of characteristics belongs to the first interpretation; the mutual cultivation of characteristics belongs to the second interpretation; and the identity of characteristics belongs to the third interpretation.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," it is further analyzed and determined through four propositions based on the *rasa* (flavor). Whether they are expanded or categorized is fully detailed in other texts; it may be understood by applying the same principles of exposition.
Since this will be explained extensively below, it is not repeated here.
Third, the judgment [of the identity] can be seen [therein].

Fourth, regarding the proof: the *Zheng* edition names them as "identical" (*ji*), whereas here they are "identical in essence" (*ti-ji*); for the three provisional [teachings] and three skillful means are identical with the one provisional [teaching] and one skillful means.
Next, regarding the explanation of "expedient means" (*upāya*): one should also say that expedient means is identical to skillful means (*kauśalya*).

Since the former is cited to explain the latter, I have not elaborated further. One should know that expedient means outside the essence is precisely the skillful means within the essence; though their names differ, once the essence underlying the name is revealed, the name upon the essence is fundamentally real. Because in the past they were divided into "outside the essence" and "within the essence," it caused the essence underlying the name to appear distinct in those two locations. Thus, we know that the "expedient means" of this sutra is the "skillful means" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the "skillful means" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the "expedient means" of this sutra—they are non-dual and without distinction.

Regarding the phrase "lowering the head" and so forth: since even the realms of humans and devas are opened [to the ultimate], how much more so the three teachings? Once they have been opened, they are non-dual and without distinction. Previously, the three layers [of the preceding sections] comprehensively governed the eight gates; although the fifth gate below concludes the provisional and the real (*kegon-jitsu*), it incidentally clarifies the threefold commentary on the chapter. The primary intent must be that the threefold commentary on the chapter pervades all eight gates. One must contemplate this without error before proceeding to provide the exegesis.

Moreover, within each of the ten pairs of every gate, each pair must be understood through three successive explanations; for throughout this entire treatise and within the teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha, nothing is presented that transcends these eight gates and ten pairs.

In the subsequent detailed explanation, the refutation of the ancient [interpretations] is first divided into four parts: first, the exposition of the errors regarding the teachings of the five periods; second, the exposition of the errors regarding the "half" and "full" [teachings]; third, the exposition of the errors regarding miscellaneous interpretations, beginning with the words "Furthermore, there are..."; and fourth, the exposition of the errors regarding derivative attachments, beginning with the words "Moreover, there are...". Since all four of these faults concern the provisional and the real—wherein the provisional is simply skillful means—how can one possibly explain this present chapter without understanding them?

Regarding the five initial "non-[times]" (*akāla*), each is first presented and then subsequently refuted. First, the initial time is presented; then, from "Now it is said" (*idānīm ucyate*) onwards, it is refuted. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the refutation of impermanence is merely a therapeutic remedy (*pratipakṣa*). Since such remedies pertain to phenomena (*dharma*) and thus lack ultimate reality, they merely establish a provisional method for a minor school. Even if there were a supreme truth (*paramārtha*), it would still not constitute a skillful means (*upāya*) for the three types of worldly consensus (*saṃvṛti*) within the practice gate. How could it possibly accord with the skillful means of provisional expediency within the supreme truth of our present teaching?

Next, regarding the refutation of the claim that the twelve years following [the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*] constitute the Prajñā period: we do not have the leisure here to refute its placement prior to the Vaipulya period; rather, we refute it on the grounds that its provisional and ultimate teachings do not transcend those of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), which is why it is described as "immediately empty" (*jìkōng*).

To cite the intent of the *Śāstra*: although the aspects of emptiness and existence may be mutually inclusive, they are still merely conceptual constructs based on the conventional; they do not yet constitute the reality within Prajñāpāramitā. If there is no reality, there can be no skillful means of identical essence—how, then, could this constitute the "Skillful Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*) of this sutra?
Question:
Do all three teachings of the *Prajñā* involve recollection and mental conception? Answer:

Since both the general and specific [aspects] refer to those who have not yet realized the truth, the text merely states that one "illuminates the emptiness within the provisional. Because emptiness has not yet been realized, it is termed "conception" (*saṃjñā*); because the mind and its objects have not yet merged, this contemplation is called "conception. Therefore, this contemplation involving conception is not the present skillful means.

Next, to explain the intent of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: within the Vaipulya [teachings], one internally illuminates the two realms of emptiness and existence through one's own practice, as it says, "One cultivates and studies the three samādhis, yet does not take these three samādhis as a realization," and so forth. To contain the ocean within a mustard seed is called a "transformation"; the meaning is that this provisional and ultimate [wisdom] surpasses the preceding *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding the refutation below the phrase "Now it is said," there are two points: first, in contrast to what preceded;
for did not the preceding teaching already involve internal illumination and external transformation?

Second, within this very section, the internal reality is termed "two" in contrast to the external; yet this is not the "Entrance into Non-duality" from the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. Since it is not non-dual, it is not the mutual identity of the Two Truths characteristic of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); how, then, could it be the skillful means of the non-duality of the provisional and the real found in the present sutra?
Furthermore, they do not know what others mean by "two" or "non-two"; therefore, this is not what is being employed here.

Next, under the section beginning with "Now I say," the argument that the *Lotus Sūtra* establishes the three, three, four, and one is refuted. This is explained in detail below in the section on "Revealing the Reality. Moreover, although it distinguishes between the provisional and the real, it does not transcend the previous teachings, because it does not speak of the provisional as being identical to the real.
Thus we know that since even the provisional and the real are separated, how much more so the partial and the small.

Next, regarding the account of his judgment on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*: previously, he held that permanence belongs only to the Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*); under the words "Now [I] say," he refutes this, arguing that although you admit the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies permanence, you nonetheless restrict that judgment to the state of Sublime Enlightenment alone.

Why is this? Since both before and after the Path, and both in the illumination of the True (zhen) and the Conventional (su), there exist both the permanent and the impermanent, how can one definitively judge the Sūtra-piṭaka based solely on the presence or absence of the term "vajra"?
Do those who attain benefit within the [Buddha] families all necessarily become Sublime Enlightened Ones?

"Measure" (māna) refers to numerical quantity as well as substantial magnitude; since those conventional objects are phenomena possessing measure, the illumination that accords with those objects is expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna).
This is refuted by means of the principles and logic of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

Therefore, the meaning of the present text is this: if one clarifies that [the Buddha-nature] is eternally abiding, then the rational nature (*rig pa'i rang bzhin*) of sentient beings is already real and already eternal; how could it only become eternal after the stage of Perfect Enlightenment?
The passage beginning with "These five periods" serves as a summary.
Therefore, the provisional and the real within those five periods are not different; neither [of these views] accords with our present intention.

Next, the section beginning with "up to" refutes the doctrines of the partial and the full based on the categories of the partial and the full, as is fully detailed in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánwén*.
Once the five periods have elapsed, all schools—both of the Half-Teaching (Hīnayāna) and the Full-Teaching (Mahāyāna)—will collapse without being attacked.
Third, from "Furthermore there are" onwards, the refutation of the *Miśra-vyākhyā* (Exegesis of the Mixed) consists of four parts:

first, a specific narration; second, a general refutation from "In this way" onwards; third, a specific refutation from "Provisionally so" onwards; and fourth, a conclusion of the error from "Each does not" onwards.
Regarding the term "locus" (*sthāna*) in the *Pṛthaktva-bhaṅga*, it refers to the locus upon which cognition relies.
Since both "that" (*er*) and "provisional" (*jia*) are terms denoting temporariness, we know that this likewise refers to a temporary locus.
The "transformed city" and the "grass hut" are illustrations of this.

As for the term "Dharma-gate," it refers to the Dharma employed by wisdom according to the specific capacities of sentient beings; because it points toward the Three Vehicles, it is called a Dharma-gate.
Regarding the term "wisdom" (*zhìnéng*): it refers to the capacity of wisdom to bestow [benefits], which exists according to whether one has progressed or not;

thus, the Three Vehicles were established at the Deer Park. "Chuí" (pronounced *zhù wěi*) may also be written as "chuí" (*zhù wéi*); it functions like a hammer that adjusts the weight of objects forward or back to achieve perfect balance. Therefore, this is the skillful efficacy of wisdom.

Regarding the statement that the four bonds do not include [the middle way], it is because the provisional and the real abide in their own respective states and do not coincide. Furthermore, since this refers only to the three vehicles in terms of both location and dharma, wisdom cannot exceed this scope; as the text does not encompass the practice and principle of the four teachings, it is said that they are "not included."
The meaning still does not encompass the teaching for the three types of persons; therefore, it is said to be "not integrated.
If one wishes to resolve this according to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) as fully presented in this chapter, what dharma would not be included?
What doctrine is not harmonized?

Regarding the four points appended as side-notes that contradict the five periods (*pañcakāla*), their arguments are for the most part based on the traditional positions established by Jiaxiang; therefore, I shall refute them in two or three places throughout this work, both above and below, so that you may discern their strengths and weaknesses.
If there were no faults, why would one turn the mind [toward the Buddha]?
Those faults exist prior to the turning of the mind; to eliminate them is to illuminate what follows.
Within this, there are three parts:

First, there is the brief establishment; second, the brief judgment from "the first two" onwards; third, the threefold triple-turning according to the truths, the teaching, and wisdom from "these various...
onwards. First, the establishment is described.

The meaning of the initial passage is as follows: since that [text] takes the first pair of wisdoms as its basis, it speaks only of "one provisional and one real. Its intent is that the provisional refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the real refers to the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*); thus, it claims that the real of the two vehicles destroys the provisional of ordinary beings, yet it fails to realize that ordinary beings do not even possess the name of "provisional."
This too is not acceptable; this [interpretation] of being attached to the Deer Park is incorrect.

Regarding the subsequent discussion on "emptiness and existence" and so forth, the intention is to simultaneously distance oneself from the aforementioned views of emptiness and existence. Here, observing emptiness without realization is taken as the provisional (expedient), while engaging with existence without defilement is taken as the real. Thus, by observing emptiness as non-empty and observing existence as non-existent, the Middle Way is revealed. This, however, is an incorrect interpretation of being attached to the Prajñāpāramitā.
This is because it is not understood that within *prajñā*, the Middle Way is not singular.
Next, regarding the phrase "emptiness and existence are internally quiescent," the intended meaning is as follows:

ceasing the tendency toward emptiness and existence, provisional and ultimate, is taken as the ultimate; taking this external application as provisional, it is not merely internally quiescent in its non-duality, but can also externally manifest dual illumination. Although the preceding [state] was non-dual, it was merely identical to internal quiescence.
This also fails to recognize that these two teachings are shared; thus, this attachment to the "neither" [position] and so forth is incorrect.
Furthermore, it maintains that this "neither-nor" and "both-yes-and-no" [approach] is still impermanent prior to the *Vajra* [Sūtra], whereas only after the *Vajra* is it truly permanent.
This is not a case of inner stillness with outer illumination; this attachment to *nirvāṇa* is incorrect.
Although this master perceived the five periods of *nirvāṇa*, he did not speak of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the ultimate truth; how much less would he exclude the "milk flavor"?
Although the general discussion comprises five sections, it is attached solely to the four periods.

Next, regarding the intent of the brief judgment: first, in order to establish the two types of wisdom directly so that one may believe in their existence, he simply cites the provisional and the real.

Regarding the subsequent generation of understanding: fundamentally, the two wisdoms are established with the intent that they be free from attachment; therefore, only by departing from the two extremes can one understand the establishment of the intent.

As for the third intent: only by departing from the two internal attachments does one fulfill the practice for oneself, and furthermore, one is able to benefit others through unattached transformative functions.

Regarding the fourth meaning: it is not merely for the benefit of others; rather, both self and other are expedient means. In its ultimate intent, the goal is fundamentally the supreme fruit; therefore, the mind at the stage immediately following the vajra-like samādhi is designated as the reality.

However, the claim that the five Buddhas do not exist within the fruit, nor as the fruit of the distant past of the "Original Gate," is logically untenable. If even ordinary beings are already revealed to be the true reality, how much more so must the stage prior to the *Vajra* [Samādhi] be judged as provisional? If the provisional were restricted solely to the period before the *Vajra*, then the Buddha would never possess provisional wisdom; how then could one explain the title of this chapter as "Expedient Means" (*upāya*)?

How much more so when they fail to judge the four grave offenses in terms of their provisional or ultimate nature, nor do they speak of the *Lotus Sūtra* at all; since this entirely deviates from my present intention, it is not to be employed.
It is called "brief" because it has already been explained in detail above.
Next, regarding the description of the three turnings, these fully traverse the Truths and so forth.
As for the term "three turnings," from the aforementioned four stages, the fourth fruit is excluded, and the preceding three are taken as the three.
This section is further divided into four parts:

first, a brief correspondence with the three turnings; second, the explanation of the reason for the turnings, beginning with "For what reason"; third, the citation of scriptural evidence, beginning with "Furthermore, it is like"; and fourth, the exposition of the underlying intention, beginning with "Moreover, gradually."
The first section also has two parts: first, the primary discussion based on the truths; second, the analogy of teaching and wisdom.
Regarding the first, "truths" refers to the two truths.
Since the provisional and the real constitute the foundation, one first uses the truths to determine the objects of cognition, which are the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).
Within this, first the headings are established, followed by a correlation with the two truths.

Although the terminology for the two truths is identical, their depths differ; specifically, the first level is judged to consist of one reality and one expedient means, which are merely termed the "two truths. Because these two truths serve as the foundation of faith, they constitute the transformation of an ordinary person into a Lesser Sage.

Regarding the subsequent emphasis on the meaning: the previous two truths are both termed "conventional," while that which transcends both is termed "ultimate"; this ultimate is merely the state of being free from attachment.
Regarding the third layer: first, "previously citing the two—emptiness and conditioned existence" cites the conventional nature of emptiness and conditioned existence;
"the non-duality of the double negation" cites the ultimate truth of the double negation.

This very reality and conventionality further transform into conventionality; therefore, it is said that both duality and non-duality are conventional, while that which is neither dual nor non-dual is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Beyond the three turnings of the fourth fruit, since the principle of "neither of the two" is the ultimate limit, there is only the mutual relation between cause and effect; because this involves the provisional and the real, it is not mentioned here.

Next, regarding the analogy for the teaching of the wise: it clarifies that these explained meanings serve as the objects of contemplation. Since there are three turnings [of the wheel], how could the means of expression and the subject of contemplation not also have three?

Next, in explaining the reason for the phrase "for the sake of people" (*wei ren*), it is said that all three layers of the two truths are adapted to the capacities of beings; since "capacity" is itself "people," and there are three types of people, this does not refer specifically to the "people" within the four *siddhāntas*.
Therefore, from beginning to end, nothing transcends the Two Truths; furthermore, as it is adapted to the capacities of beings, it is also called "the person.

Regarding the citation of evidence: the words of the Constantly Abiding [Tathāgata] do not exceed these three. Thus, by addressing only these, he again provides the basis upon which Buddhism relies, thereby corroborating the previous intent regarding the application of the Truths.

Next, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, the Buddha's teaching" reiterates the general intent as a proof, specifically to corroborate the preceding discussion on the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*).
Since what is described within the teachings does not exceed these three, they are called the "three gates"; here, the teachings themselves constitute the gates.

Next, from "Furthermore, gradually" onwards, the text summarizes the preceding three—the Truths, the Teachings, and Wisdom—in terms of the Buddha’s intention for conversion (*parāvṛtti*). This intention, both in its objective and subjective aspects, does not transcend these three. First, it causes ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to abandon existence (*bhava*) and enter emptiness (*śūnyatā*); this refers to the initial establishment of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Second, it destroys the attachment to emptiness held by the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), whereby both emptiness and existence are abandoned;

this refers to the intention regarding the small Bodhisattvas. Although they have abandoned both emptiness and existence, they likely have not yet perceived the Middle Way (*madhyama*). Regarding the ancient commentaries on "Bodhisattva," they distinguish between Great and Small solely based on their respective stages (*avasthā*), without considering whether or not one knows the Middle Way.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "Or perhaps," the simultaneous disappearance of both the Middle and the Extremes refers to a Great Bodhisattva; alternatively, it may indicate those at the eighth, first, or tenth stages, or the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "This is for," he further uses the five vehicles to judge the intent behind his transformative teaching.
The meaning is this:

the Buddha’s intention in transforming beings during his lifetime did not exceed the Five Vehicles. Within the first three layers, ordinary people were established as the Human and Celestial Vehicle; those who gave rise to faith and, by breaking through existence, entered emptiness were established as the Two Vehicles.

Next, the section beginning with "Furthermore, for the sake of" analyzes [the path] by means of the three provisional designations (trividha-prajñapti). This appears to refer to a person practicing in successive stages who first breaks through the three provisional designations; herein, one additional instance of the three provisional designations is added, while otherwise there is no difference from the rest.

This merely refers to the differentiation of the aforementioned five vehicles; since the initial refutation of existence must necessarily involve the three types of provisional constructs (*trividha-prajñapti*), the first [vehicle] takes these three provisional constructs as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and all other intentions are identical.
Although the various previous versions do not explicitly state "provisional," it must be understood that the first level of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is necessarily provisional.

Furthermore, the fact that the preceding versions do not mention the "first level" was originally intended for the cultivation of the Middle Way (madhyamaka), but the text was merely abbreviated; therefore, the refutation of the provisional to cultivate the Middle Way is largely the intention of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* masters.

The third level should be described as "not threefold conventionality": emptiness and existence constitute duality, while neither emptiness nor existence constitutes non-duality; duality and non-duality constitute the conventional, while neither duality nor non-duality constitutes the ultimate. This can be understood by analogy with what preceded it, and thus is not stated again.
"Now, in detail," and below, merely provide a general and concise refutation.

This is further divided into five parts: first, a brief negation; second, "The Sūtra says," and below, citing the text to demonstrate the point correctly; third, "Furthermore, regarding the beginning," and below, concluding the negation to reveal the fault; fourth, "As by Vasubandhu," and below, citing an example; fifth, "It should be known," and below, providing the final summary.

Regarding the initial passage: it employs the intent of the other five periods as a supplementary framework, while concealing the names of those five periods to serve as a latent commentary for its own explanation.

Now, by discussing horizontally within each period the extent of the provisional, the real, and their functional applications, the intention is to clarify the inconceivable and skillful employment of the Tathāgata; yet because this skillful employment does not establish itself as a fixed system but only constitutes a gradual progression, it is said to be "not so."

Subsequently, according to the three turnings and further excluding the stage of fruition, the intention was to model this after the detachment from attachment through the wisdom of the truths, using the cause to manifest the fruit; yet, unintentionally, it also resulted in the fallacy of gradualism.

Next, regarding the citation of the text to provide the correct demonstration: now, by employing the mutual inclusion of the eight teachings across the five periods, they together constitute the One Real Teaching. Within each period, the teachings are intermingled both horizontally and vertically; however, it is only upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra* that the wisdom of the Truth becomes pure and singular. Nevertheless, this [chapter] still distinguishes and establishes the characteristics of the provisional means (*upāya*). Therefore, at the very beginning of the section on provisional means, it praises the five Buddhas’ wisdom and the truth of their provisional means. For this reason, the title of this chapter must rely upon the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
The Sūtra says: "All shall behold you, even unto the fruit, which is eternal.
The Sūtra instructs one to abandon expedient means, yet you instead employ them once again.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* itself designates the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the ultimate; you, however, point only to the final moment of mind in the *Vajracchedikā*, thereby opening up all other teachings while simultaneously discarding them.

Next, regarding the passage showing the error which says, "The fruit of transformation through faith and understanding," this refers to the gradual entry from beginning to end through the four preceding stages. Following this, the section beginning with "What does it have to do with...
correctly demonstrates that [the opponent's position] is incorrect.

Therefore, Jiashang further stated: "The body and the vehicle each constitute four propositions. Regarding the four propositions of the vehicle: first, three are expedient means and one is the ultimate truth, intended to cause one to abandon the three and adopt the one. Although those who follow the teachings may abandon the three, they remain attached to the single reality; thus, while coarse delusions are removed, subtle delusions immediately arise."
Now, I ask: if they have already abandoned the three [vehicles] by the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly, then at what point is the single reality (ekayāna) established?
If they have not yet reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there was no teaching prior to that which spoke of abandoning the three.
For a śrāvaka prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, views and cultivation have long been destroyed; yet upon reaching this [sūtra], what kind of subtle delusions arise?
Under which category of delusion is this attachment to reality subsumed?
How could there be subtle delusions arising from hearing the Dharma?
It continues: "In order to refute [opposing views], it is clarified that both the three and the one are expedient means."

Now I ask: I do not yet understand whether these three [teachings] are all skillful means prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or whether they have already reached the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Prior to this, it was still said that the "three" were expedient means; when had it ever been stated that the "one" was also an expedient means?

Therefore, at the beginning of this chapter, it merely says, "In the past, expedient means were shown as three. There is absolutely no statement that both "one" and "three" are equally called expedient means. As for the words used to refute [the opponent's view], in what context would they be applicable?
The third person says:
"Those who receive the teaching recognize that both 'the three' and 'the one' are expedient means; they further seal them as 'neither' and take this to be the ultimate principle.
Now I ask: among the three turnings [of the wheel], which turning contains the text regarding "neither"?
Prior to this, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) did not even possess the former two [realizations], let alone the "neither-nor" (ubhayānta-vinirmukta).
If bodhisattvas were already able to enter [the truth] at every stage, what need would there have been for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

Third, again, taking three as one constitutes duality; the negation of both constitutes non-duality. Both duality and non-duality are expedient means (*upāya*); that which is neither dual nor non-dual is the reality (*tattva*). The refutation follows the same principle as the previous inquiry into the person and the location.

Fourth: "The two, non-duality, and the negation of both still belong to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); they cannot avoid being mere conventional designations (*vyavahāra*) and skillful means (*upāya*). That all phenomena are quiescent and ineffable is the ultimate reality (*tattva*)."
Now, regarding the question: when the samādhi ends and the teaching is announced, and the fundamental source is revealed through the three cycles, is this being taught or not?
The meaning of quiescent extinction is universal; why should it be limited to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* alone?

The principle underlying the teachings is fundamentally beyond words; how much more so for that which is "Great" and unspeakable? Previously, for the sake of the five bhikṣus, [the Buddha] spoke of the unspeakable; how much more so now, where the five Buddhas extensively clarify the opening of provisional means and the discernment of the provisional and the real? Once the provisional and the real are thus revealed, who would still cling to mere words?

Regarding the statement that there are "three seals," this refers to being deluded by the teachings and deluded by one's own sentiments; now, as we judge the teachings according to their respective sections, the provisional names must have a definitive point of reference for their resolution—how could they merely be used to dismiss words?
To pursue word after word leaves delusion ultimately unremoved; though one may refute [the opponent] a thousand or ten thousand times, it can never be exhausted.
The four propositions regarding the body should be understood according to this principle.

Furthermore, since the title at the beginning of this chapter is "Skillful Means" (*upāya*), one should employ skillful means to explain this chapter; to provide an explanation based on [the notion of] substantial reality (*bhūta-artha*) is a grave departure from the chapter's heading. Thus we know that Jiaxiang (Jizang) was bathed in the sublime transformation and his mind was already irrigated by its meaning. While the old commentaries have been circulated first, they must be thoroughly refuted in accordance with reason. Recognizing this great purport, the relationship between teacher and disciple may be perfected.
By this same principle, the other cases may also be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the three kinds of Dharma wheels which differ in their transmission, the Great Master [Nāgārjuna] termed them "Sudden" and "Milk," naming them after their fundamental source; the Great Master [Zhiyi] took the Three Samādhis as the branches and twigs, yet they likewise take the *amṛta* (clarified butter) as their ultimate return to the root.

Now, regarding the question: generally speaking, that which is called the "root" (mūla) is said to be that which can produce; it is produced at the beginning and subsequently subsumed back into the root. Yet, the root itself is not the beginning. These two statements are mutually contradictory. If the branches and the root do not stand together, then subsumption is likewise inappropriate. Furthermore, if the root and the branches are divided into two, they are only unified through subsumption; one is the root and two are named branches. Thus, the root would originally have been branches. One must therefore reconcile the initial [state] with the subsequent [state]; hence, the distinct branches of the *Avataṃsaka* are opened up so as to enter the fundamental perfection of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Moreover, since both the distinct and the perfect teachings of the *Avataṃsaka* constitute proximate traces (*upāya*), the meaning of the "root" is further sublated, and the fundamental [truth] of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is established.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that the three *samādhis* are merely branches and secondary elements: this may be acceptable in the case of the Deer Park;
however, how could it apply to the two *sūtras*?
If the two *sūtras* were merely secondary and distinct branches, how could the *Avataṃsaka* possibly constitute the fundamental essence?
If that were so, it would merely result in bringing the trunk back to the trunk, or bringing the branches back to the branches.
If the Lotus Sūtra had no connection with the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, then the two texts would remain eternally distinct; how, then, could it be called "bringing the branches back to the root"?

Moreover, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* section, there is no text concerning entry into the *Avataṃsaka*, but only entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa* provides explicit textual evidence for the ultimate culmination of the five flavors. If the original master’s teachings were to be altered, then if one persists with the old [system], the relationship of teacher and disciple cannot be established, the doctrine of "receiving [the teaching] upon the chest" would have no application, and where could the words of "reverently wearing [it on the head]" be placed?
Regarding the citation of two passages as examples, these are of the same category as the "expedient means within the essence" (*tǐnèi fāngbiàn*) found in the present sutra.
As for the ten kinds of expedient means in the *Mahāyānopāya-kauśalya-sūtra*, they have not yet been examined.
5. From "One should know" onwards, the section concludes by demonstrating the refutation of erroneous views.

The phrase "like space or the ocean" encompasses the streams of form (*rūpa-srotas*) found in all sutras, showing that they all ultimately converge within the ocean of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samudra*) of this present sutra.
From "Now, to clarify" onwards is the formal explanation, which is divided into two parts:
first, the general, and second, the specific.
The first section has three parts:

First is the enumeration, second is the explanation, and third, from "If all dharmas" onwards, the functional efficacy of the Dharma is analyzed by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Within the explanation, each of the four statements first presents a heading and is subsequently interpreted by quoting the relevant text.

Regarding the first phrase, since the cited text states "all phenomena" (*dharmas*) and so forth, it is provisionally spoken of in terms of existence because of the use of the term "existence"; yet this term "existence" does not transcend the thousand suchnesses and hundred realms.

Regarding the second sentence: it frequently cites five passages, all of which testify to the entry into reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, "reality" is explained here in contrast to "entry and testimony.

The first passage expresses the intention of [the Buddha] adapting to the capacities of sentient beings; the second passage is the foundation of all dharmas; the third passage is the core of the pedagogical method (*naya*); the fourth passage is the source of fundamental practice; and the fifth passage is the principle of transcending teachings.
All texts take entry into realization as the reality; thus, we know that whether there is verbal expression or non-expression, all are fundamentally based upon the truth.
Regarding the intent of the citation in the third sentence: all phenomena are provisional, while the true mark (*dharmatā*) is the reality.

The "real" corresponds to the second phrase and the "expedient" corresponds to the first; these two phrases combined constitute the third, because there is no distinct dharma apart from the first two gates.

The passage beginning with "For example" cites an illustration: it is "empty" because it is a mental construct, and "real" because it counteracts desire. Since this single contemplation is both real and empty, what prevents a single dharma from being both expedient and real?

Regarding the fourth phrase, the cited text refers directly to the Middle Way (madhyamaka). The two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—are equal in their principle and difficult to conceive; by negating both of these truths, the wondrous Middle is revealed. Furthermore, this does not differ from the previous three gates, for since the principles of all four gates are identical, they are all described as "all-encompassing."
Third, from "If all" onwards, the functional utility is elucidated. This section further consists of two parts:
first, the direct elucidation of the functional utility of the phrases in encompassing phenomena; second, from "Directly listing" onwards, the meaning of those phrases is clarified.

Regarding the initial passage: if even these four phrases mutually encompass and mutually refute one another—whereby the provisional is entirely provisional, and so on, up to being neither provisional nor real—how much more so must other dharmas be encompassed and refuted?
Moreover, since there is no further dharma outside of the four propositions, it is only in this way that the refutation and establishment of the present sutra are fully realized;

how could they possibly be the same as the refutations and establishments of the various masters? One should know that these masters do not recognize the various provisional and real [teachings]; even if they speak of the real, because they have not yet distinguished it, the meaning of the real is not established. How much more so when they look at one another and mutually speculate, remaining deluded regarding the real? Therefore, they are all refuted by the first proposition, which is why it says, "There is nothing that is not provisional."
If even the first case is thus, how much more so the three?
Therefore, while the various masters have attained both the provisional and the real, they have only grasped a small portion of the provisional.
As for the phrase "that which the Tathāgata has taught," this cites the fruit to illustrate the case of ordinary beings.

Even that which the Buddha has spoken is all provisional; how much more so in the final age, when people speak at random, claiming their own words to be true, failing to contemplate the Sage’s transformation while seeking only to promote their own ordinary selves.
As for the second phrase, "reality" refers to the ultimate.
If even the provisional teachings spoken by the Buddha must ultimately enter into the ultimate reality, how much more so for other provisional and ultimate teachings that would not do so?
Therefore, one should know that all things consist of only one single reality.
Regarding the term "nest and cave" (*cháo kū*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"Where birds dwell in trees, it is called a nest; where beasts dwell in burrows, it is called a cave.
"To preserve" (*hō*) means to cling to and dwell within.
To exhaustively comprehend the great purport, one must accord with the Buddha-mind; yet to directly adhere to a single corner is like preserving a nest or a cave.
The second and third sets of four phrases may be understood by analogy; therefore, every phrase in this text is all-pervasive.

If one were to condense them so they may be easily recognized, they consist simply of the three wisdoms illuminating the objects of the three truths and responding to three types of capacities. Because these capacities, phenomena, principles, and events are all-pervasive, it can be known that everything is "all. This is because when one is empty, all are empty, and thus all are real; when one is provisional, all are provisional, and thus all are expedient. The second and third sets of four phrases represent the Middle Wisdom’s simultaneous illumination and simultaneous non-illumination. Internally, because the three virtues and three bodies are fully present, their external application manifests horizontally and vertically through both the explicit and the secret. To fulfill the intent of this sutra’s refutation and establishment—contrasting it with the past—it is necessary to formulate these four sets of phrases.

While this is the general outline of the dharma-characteristics, when discussed specifically, this present chapter pertains solely to the third [stage]. Furthermore, half of the provisional [teachings] is termed the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-paṛiccheda), as it is spoken in contrast to the realized wisdom of self-attestation.

Therefore, it must be stated that the third half-verse still requires the inclusion of those remaining three and a half [verses] within this one half-verse; only then can it be designated as the present "Chapter on Expedient Means."

If even the exclusive adherence to each of the four propositions, while claiming to encompass everything, does not constitute a universal principle, how much less so for the various masters who universally conceptualize provisional teachings? Therefore, it is said: "One must not hold to a single-sided view."

Regarding the next section, "Direct Enumeration" (*zhíliè*), which clarifies the meaning of the phrases: although the preceding explanations have briefly cited and glossed the characteristics of the text, they still constitute a direct enumeration to define the features of the phrases; they have not yet reached a comprehensive integration to discuss the profound intent (*xuánzhǐ*). Since both refutation and establishment have already been exhaustively treated—neither partial toward a single phrase nor obstructed by a single corner—it is said, "It is already like this," let alone when viewed from afar through its grand principles.
Because it does not confine itself to a single direction, it is called "Profound Observation" (*xuánlǎn*).
"Direction" refers to a single person or a single practice;

that is to say, regarding a single principle or a single teaching, it establishes and subsumes them as they arise, and refutes and dissolves them as they appear, being free and sovereign in its taking and rejecting—hence it is called "Vast and Expansive" (*kuàngdàng*). Because it ascends out of stagnation and obscurity, it is called "Sublime and Luminous" (*gāomíng*).

Furthermore, exhausting the far-reaching teachings is called "remote observation" (yáoguān); examining the profound principles is termed "mysterious insight" (xuánlǎn); employing horizontal pervasiveness is termed "vast and expansive" (kuàngdàng); and pointing to vertical penetration is termed "lofty and brilliant" (gāomíng). Because it elucidates the comprehensive integration of our own school, it says, "it is like this."
If one considers the meaning of the character "hanging" (xuán), its significance can also be seen; since others do not perceive this, how could they possibly explain the "Expedient Means" chapter?
As for the phrase "how much more so regarding the purport of the treatise," it is intended to refute the errors of past [scholars].

For the time being, by means of the provisional and the real within the characteristics of the teachings—refuting and establishing, opening and bestowing, appearing and disappearing, expanding and contracting, practicing and storing—it discusses both practice and realization, as well as self and other, in a combined exposition.
Examining Xiang’s writings to discuss their underlying intent, and summarizing his points to clarify their significance:

one must understand that the four phrases refer to nothing other than the single *dharmatā*. This *dharmatā* is none other than true suchness (*tathatā*), the real mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and suchness-nirvāṇa (*tathatā-nirvāṇa*).
Because the essence of *dharmatā* does not conflict with all phenomena, it does not receive them, does not abide in them, and does not enter into them.
Therefore, each individual name, each mental dharma, each verse, each cause and effect, each ordinary being and sage,
and each environment and its inhabitants— even these ten pairs— are none other than the Dharma-realm;
their meaning can be established as sovereign and unimpeded, just as it is explained in the *Twenty Gates*.

Whether in its origin or its conclusion, the essence and principle are no different; thus, that which is spoken is as if unspoken, and that which is unspoken is as if spoken. Its illumination of the nature [of reality] is not remote, being sovereign and infinite. Although it is infinite, it does not transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); yet these four propositions are themselves without propositions, and being without propositions, they constitute propositions. Each and every proposition universally encompasses the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions. However, prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, each teaching and each proposition had not yet been fully realized; only upon arriving at this assembly do they become of one flavor, without distinction, and so forth.

This is exactly as explained in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs": where there is difference, there is no difference; where there is no difference, there is difference. To explain the individual chapters following this:
having already understood that all dharmas are mutually fused and universally interpenetrating, when one speaks of the Real, the Expedient is contained within that Real;

it is precisely by pointing to this Expedient that it is named the "Expedient Means Chapter. When one speaks of the Expedient, it is the inconceivable Expedient; because this Expedient possesses the Real, it is precisely by means of this Expedient that it is named the "Expedient Means Chapter. When one speaks of both the Expedient and the Real, each has its own point of convergence. This is the "both" of mutual identity and the "both" of subsuming the three [truths]; therefore, it is named the "Expedient Means Chapter."

Therefore, taking the skillful means that are themselves reality as the "Chapter on Skillful Means" (Upāya-paṛivarta), the presentation of that which is neither provisional nor real is simply the principle of skillful means; since this principle encompasses all three propositions, they are all included within the "Chapter on Skillful Means."
Question:
If that is so, since every sentence is pervasive and every sentence belongs to the category of skillful means, why must it be the third? Answer:
First is "convenience of name," because it possesses both the provisional and the real;
second is "convenience of meaning," because that which is subsumed therein is universal.

In other cases, there is convenience of meaning but not of name; and although the remaining three possess both provisional meaning and provisional names, they do not equal the third, where the name itself is identical to the possession [of both]. By employing this very reality as the provisional, it constitutes the present chapter.

Therefore, in the ten pairs that follow, each pair possesses both the names "expedient" (upāya) and "real" (bhūta); all take the identity of the real as the expedient to constitute the "Expedient Means" chapter. This is especially so since the first three general explanations are each headed by ten textual passages and eight gates.

If it were not so, then the matters of skillful means (*upāya*), principle (*li*), and even the *siddhānta* would not be included among the names of the dharmic characteristics listed under skillful means; nor would they constitute the ten meanings of "original" (*hon*) and "traces" (*seki*) of this present sutra. Although these ten meanings appear distinct in their original and traced aspects, they are inconceivably one; although the original and traces differ, the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is one and the same. For the sake of sentient beings, the sequence of exposition—from the listing and explanation of the arising [of the teaching] down to the original and traces—is presented; yet while the phenomena, principles, and even the *siddhāntas* differ, one who grasps the intent forgets the words, and through verbal expression attains liberation. If one perceives this intent, then silence and speech are always non-contradictory; taking this very principle as the object of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one causes that object to become clearly visible. That none of the other commentaries possess this is precisely due to this reason.

If even this interpretation is feared to be flawed, how much more so those of various schools that are partial, superficial, and isolated? Even if they list many dharmalakṣaṇas, it is difficult to distinguish between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; and while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was not yet revealed at the time of their doctrinal classifications, if one were to claim that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shares the same flavor as other teachings, where would the words of the "threefold teaching" (the three turnings of the wheel) be found? They would have no basis whatsoever.

Nevertheless, among these eight [sections], the first seven constitute the Trace Gate (jìmén) and the eighth constitutes the Origin Gate (běnmén). Although the Origin has not yet been reached, the principle of the provisional and the real (quánshí) is pervasive; therefore, the subsequent text states: "This is my skillful means (fāngbiàn), and all Buddhas are likewise."

Therefore, the term "expedient means" (upāya) applies to both the fundamental and the phenomenal; since this profound interpretation differs from other ways of analyzing the text, it does not accord with Guangzhai’s method of delimiting phrases.

Furthermore, regarding the intended sequence of these eight gates: if the names were not listed, there would be no basis for explanation; if they were not introduced, one would be confused regarding the order of exposition. Explanation serves to correctly demonstrate the characteristics of the ten textual passages; citation of evidence serves to prevent those who might lack faith; the conclusion serves to clarify the original intent of the chapter; and the detailed analysis serves to ensure that the interpretation of the chapter has a clear point of reference. By delimiting and explaining, one comes to know where the coarse and the subtle reside. Only in this way are the profound purports of the chapter fully revealed.

Furthermore, by pre-emptively clarifying the fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku), one comes to recognize the original ground, the provisional and the real, and self and other; only then can the Great Path of the long-term and short-term transformations be revealed.

Within the enumeration of names, each must be designated with the terms "provisional" or "real," such as saying "phenomena and principle: provisional and real," or even "siddhānta: provisional and real. This means that phenomena are provisional while principle is real, and so forth, up to the threefold provisionality and single reality of the siddhāntas. Furthermore, by classifying these through the three types of explanations for the chapter title, the skillful means (*upāya*) of the present sutra is established.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* states:
"From this point downward, the causal and resultant aspects of this sutra are revealed.

Thus, among the ten pairs, the first five proceed from cause to fruit, while the latter five represent the superior functions of the fruit. Furthermore, the text of this entire work may also be divided into cause and fruit according to its provisional and ultimate (honji-suijaku) dimensions; hence we know that if the former four were absent within the cause, the meaning of the cause would be shallow and narrow, and if the latter five were absent, the function of the fruit would be crude and mundane.

Among these, the teaching is the sacred transformation; it is designated by the name of its recipient. This differs from worldly people who regard the teaching as the cause and the Buddha’s wisdom as the fruit, and it also differs from other systems such as those of the three or four [vehicles].
The remainder is as explained below in the section on the provisional and the real (*keuan-shih*).

Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yun-yun*) following the discussion on arising, one should describe the characteristics of arising for each respective chapter; these can be seen by searching carefully.

Furthermore, since the textual indicators of the "capable" (the subject) must correspond to the "object" (the transformed), among the five subsequent pairs, only one within the category of essence and function corresponds to the object; the remaining four all derive their names from the "capable" that they correspond to.
Furthermore, this is also identical to the ten sublime meanings; were it not so, who would know that the skillful means must comprise these ten dharmas?
And who would know that the meaning of these ten dharmas pervades the entire sutra?

If these ten dharmas were absent, the text of the sūtra would fail to elucidate cause and effect as well as the subjective and objective; therefore, it is only when all ten pairs exhaustively reach the essential point that they constitute the ten pairs of this present sūtra.

If that is so, then the entire sutra from beginning to end is designated as "expedient means" (*upāya*), referring collectively to the preceding teachings as that which is being opened up; only then can it be said that this sutra is an expedient means. Thus we know that the "Expedient Means" in the Prologue consists of the expedients of certification, faith, and the incitement [of the teaching]; the "Parable" is merely the expedient of analogy; the "Causes and Conditions" is merely the expedient of the past; the "Original Gate" is merely the expedient of the long distant past; and the "Circulation" is merely the expedient of the universal Dharma of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is because of these expedients that it is called "Reality."

If one attains this insight, it will be as clear as viewing fruit in the palm of one's hand; the entirety of the *Lotus Sūtra* can be known within a square inch of the heart, and the entire gateway of the teachings throughout a single lifetime can be recognized in a single kṣaṇa. Cause and effect, self and others, are all realized as a single Dharma; throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, there is no longer any seeking of divergent paths.

If one examines this through the vehicle of the ten dharmas, the Samādhi of the Lotus Sutra will find a firm footing, and the distant journey toward the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood can be anticipated; may all you wise ones who possess the eye of wisdom deign to observe this.
The Record of the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra, Scroll Three, Part Two.
